extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, judges, and practitioners (and advanced law students)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative criteria and standards for when courts should vacate, remand, or otherwise remedy agency rulemakings or orders—with particular attention to notice-and-comment failures, inadequate explanations, Chenery-related issues, and the role of harmless-error/prejudice inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-cause exception cannot rest on bald assertions
rubrics_metrics.description: “Bald assertions that the agency does not believe comments would be useful cannot create good cause to forgo notice and comment procedures.” (D.C. Circuit language addressing CAB’s invocation of the good-cause exception.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should reject conclusory agency claims that further comment is unnecessary; an agency invoking §553(b)’s good-cause exception must show why notice-and-comment is impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest. Examples: D.C. Circuit invalidated CAB’s second issuance where the agency simply asserted further comments would be unhelpful. Where the agency supplies concrete reasons and engagement with stakeholders, the good-cause claim is weaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstration of prejudice required before automatic vacatur
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of presuming harm, insist on a demonstration of prejudice before invalidating agency rules for procedural failures (i.e., require a showing that challengers were actually harmed by lack of notice-and-comment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the party challenging an agency action had a full and fair opportunity to voice objections, whether the agency heard and considered the substantive concerns the party would have raised, and whether there is substantial reason to think additional comments would have led the agency to change its decision. Positive example: D.C. Circuit treated notice-and-comment error as harmless in U.S. Telecom Ass’n v. FCC because challengers had already raised and debated the same arguments. Courts should conduct a context-sensitive inquiry into prejudice rather than treating notice-and-comment errors as structural per se reversible error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common lower-court harmlessness standard (stringent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many lower courts apply that the “failure to provide notice and comment is harmless only where the agency’s mistake clearly had no bearing on the procedure used or the substance of decision reached.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read literally, this standard makes it nearly impossible to find notice-and-comment failures harmless because skipping notice necessarily “bears on the procedure used.” The standard forces agencies into a dilemma: they must argue they would not have changed their minds (but that undermines the premise of an open-minded notice-and-comment process). The article criticizes this inflexible formulation and proposes instead a prejudice-focused inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider agency's prior engagement with regulated parties as evidence of notice/lack of prejudice
rubrics_metrics.description: Where agencies have maintained close working relationships with regulated communities (meetings, internet bulletins, soliciting input), that engagement can show actual notice and diminish claims of prejudice from formal notice-and-comment defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete communications—publication of anticipated technical corrections, direct meetings with industry stakeholders, and explicit statements that a prior textual provision was an error—can undercut challenges that there was no opportunity to comment. Example: EPA’s interactions with USWAG/GE over a porous-surface PCB rule undermined plaintiffs’ claim they lacked a chance to comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt Clean Air Act-style prejudice standard for procedural errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory standard: invalidate an agency action for procedural errors “only if the errors were so serious and related to matters of such central relevance to the rule that there is a substantial likelihood that the rule would have been significantly changed if such errors had not been made.” (42 U.S.C. § 7607(d)(8)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts could use this as a model gloss on the APA’s prejudicial-error rule to require remedial restraint: look for a substantial likelihood of a materially different rule absent the procedural error before ordering vacatur. This standard asks for a context-sensitive inquiry into centrality and likely effect, rather than automatic invalidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review the whole record when assessing prejudice, but guard against undisclosed bases
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA instructs reviewing courts to review “the whole record.” Outside formal proceedings, that record may include whatever influenced the agency’s decisionmaking; accordingly, courts may sometimes look beyond the notice-and-comment administrative record when determining prejudice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While courts generally confine inquiry to the notice-and-comment record to prevent agencies from relying on undisclosed materials (which would undermine notice), once a procedural deficiency is identified the remedial inquiry can permissibly consider extrarecord materials that bear on whether parties were prejudiced. Balance: permit useful extrarecord inquiry while protecting the notice function by preventing agencies from manufacturing justificatory materials post hoc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh costs of remedial purity vs. benefits when selecting remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Vacatur and strict remedial purity impose costs (agency carelessness risk, administrative delay, expense); courts should weigh these costs against the systemic benefits that prophylactic rules produce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that remand-and-vacate may be wasteful where the likelihood of a materially different outcome is small or where the agency can quickly and predictably reinstate a rule. The article urges courts to consider proportionality and real-world costs rather than reflexively invalidating agency actions for procedural imperfections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chenery injunction against judicial substitution of reasons (scope and purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chenery: review should be “confined . . . to a judgment upon the validity of the grounds upon which the [agency] itself based its action,” and courts generally may not uphold agency action on alternative grounds the agency did not rely on at decision time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chenery’s core rationale is to incentivize agencies to adopt general rules and to supply contemporaneous, nonarbitrary reasons; it functions prophylactically. But Chenery is not an absolute bar to remedial flexibility—its purpose (forcing agencies to give reasons, encouraging rulemaking) should be weighed against the costs of vacatur in particular cases. The article analogizes to Miranda exceptions to show that prophylactic rules can be confined when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context-sensitive exceptions to Chenery’s prophylaxis
rubrics_metrics.description: Chenery need not be absolute; courts can, in some contexts, decline automatic vacatur where the systemic benefits of insisting on contemporaneous agency reasoning are outweighed by the costs of reversal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous to Miranda’s limited exceptions (traffic stops, public-safety questions, impeachment), administrative law can allow targeted exceptions where exclusion (vacatur) would produce disproportionate costs and little systemic benefit. The inquiry should ask whether vacatur truly advances Chenery’s incentive goals in the particular circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate between core/explanatory defects and subsidiary factual errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge Friendly’s proposal: Chenery’s rule should apply to cases where an agency supplied a wrong or unexplained reason for its decision (core policy/rationale), but not where the agency erred on subsidiary factual findings that are supported by adequate alternative facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vacatur is appropriate to force agencies to clarify central policy choices (“Do you really mean it?”). But courts should avoid vacating for subsidiary factual mistakes when adequate alternative facts support the outcome and there is no reason to think the agency would materially change course if apprised of the error. This reduces needless expense and delay in complex technical cases (e.g., ratemaking).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prill-related criterion: failure to resolve statutory ambiguities forfeits deference
rubrics_metrics.description: When an agency acts pursuant to an erroneous view of law and thus fails to exercise the discretion delegated to it by Congress, judicial deference (Chevron) is not accorded (Prill principle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the agency genuinely failed to recognize or exercise interpretive discretion. But bear in mind three moderating features: (1) agencies often adopt pragmatic readings and may truly prefer the chosen interpretation; (2) agencies can frequently reinstate the decision on remand; and (3) statutory ambiguities may be marginal or debatable, making vacatur for failure to explicate every alternative interpretive possibility excessive. Examples: PDK Labs. (DEA) and Postal Regulatory Commission rate cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not punish agencies for failing to address marginal or implausible alternative readings
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should be cautious in rebuking agencies for not ventilating marginally plausible alternative statutory constructions that the agency reasonably believed unavailable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the agency’s chosen reading is functional and the agency has acted consistently with it (and explained its view), remanding for failure to discuss unlikely alternatives produces little added-value and risks boilerplate responses. Consider whether the agency’s conduct (e.g., exercising the power at issue) demonstrates a genuine preference that is unlikely to change on remand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heightened remedial concern where agency relied on undisclosed technical studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may apply a heightened prejudice standard and be less willing to treat procedural errors as harmless when the agency relied on studies or technical bases that it failed to disclose during the notice-and-comment process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failures to reveal portions of the technical basis for a proposed rule in time for meaningful commentary represent serious procedural error (e.g., Pers. Watercraft Indus.; Small Refiner Lead Phase-Down Task Force). In such cases, vacatur or remand may be appropriate because nondisclosure meaningfully undermines the notice-and-comment purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedial discretion includes alternatives to vacatur (e.g., remand without vacatur)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because vacatur is not always necessary to vindicate procedural norms, courts can consider less drastic remedies (such as remand without vacatur) when challengers cannot show prejudice or when public interest and costs counsel against invalidation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited (and analogous cases) show courts sometimes preserve agency action while requiring corrective procedures (redoing an EIS but upholding leases, as in Pub. Emps. for Envtl. Responsibility v. Hopper). Remedy selection should account for likelihood of successful reinstatement, public-interest harms from vacatur, and whether the agency can cure defects without unsettling settled reliance interests.
